title: Expect to be laughed at
hookLine: take up philosophy and some will mock you; hold to what seems best (Enchiridion 22)

lines: OH, SO YOU'RE A PHILOSOPHER NOW.
cards: A sibling rolls their eyes. A friend says, oh, so you're a philosopher now. A coworker catches you breathing at your desk and makes a joke about it.
After almost a year of this practice, pausing before you answer, sitting for two minutes in the morning, saying a line under your breath at the stoplight, someone was bound to notice.
Section twenty-two of the handbook has a line for this, and it could almost be your sibling talking. Epictetus warned his students to expect it.

teach.h: GET READY TO BE LAUGHED AT.
teach.b: If you want philosophy, section twenty-two says, get ready from the start to be laughed at. Many will mock you. They'll say: he's come back to us a philosopher all of a sudden.
And: where did he get that superior look?

The Greek for that look is ophrys, literally the eyebrow, the raised brow of someone who thinks they're above it all. And here Epictetus turns to his own students first. Don't put on that look, he says.
The mockers may be rude, but don't hand them a reason.

teach.h: HOLD TO IT, LIKE A POST.
teach.b: Instead, hold to what seems best to you, as someone posted to that place by God. The image is a soldier at a post, not showing off, just staying.
Readers who don't share Epictetus' belief in God can still hear the shape of it: a commitment you keep quietly, because it's yours to keep. Then the two endings.
If you stay with it, he says, the same people who laughed at first will come to admire you.
But if you give in to them, you'll be laughed at twice. He might be too hopeful about the first; some people never stop teasing.
But the second rings true: dropping a practice because of a joke rarely ends the joking. It just adds a new one. So: no raised eyebrow, no speeches about your new morning routine.
Just keep doing it, kindly, and let the laughter be weather.

how: Some people who take up a philosophical or spiritual practice keep it quietly, without explaining or showing off, and let teasing pass.

o: Greek for a raised eyebrow, a superior look
a Greek word for a mocking laugh or jeer
a soldier's post he must never abandon

games.q: expect to be laughed at — tap the pairs.
p: a philosopher all of a sudden!

s: Epictetus tells his students to argue back with the mockers
he tells them not to put on a superior look, and to hold to what seems best.
the Greek word for a superior look literally means the eyebrow
he says if you give in, you'll be laughed at twice
once for starting, once for quitting.

games.q: your family teases you about your new practice. what does Epictetus say to do?
o: explain it at length over dinner.
keep at it quietly, without a superior look.
games.why: don't put on airs, he says; hold to what seems best. those who laughed may later admire you; quit, and you're laughed at twice.

practice: Choose one small practice from this year that you want to keep, a pause, a line, a sit, a walk, and picture doing it today in front of whoever is most likely to tease you.
Hear the joke, and notice the urge to explain, or to quit, or to look superior. Let all three go, and see yourself just doing the practice, quietly, and carrying on with your day.

wordCard.voice: Ophrys. The Greek word for a raised eyebrow, the superior look Epictetus warned his students not to wear; some will mock, so don't put on airs, and hold to what seems best. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 22: philosophy, the thing the students have taken up.

carryVoice: Your line: hold to it. A joke passes, and the practice quietly stays. See you tomorrow.
